title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (4 of 7)
word: the story of the gods and Brahman
hook: whoever thinks they know it doesn't
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eye does not go there. That by which the eyes see, know that alone as Brahman. Your line, the one behind the ear. Day two hundred forty-two.

At one end of the dinner table, a cousin who has taken one philosophy class and now has the universe figured out. At the other end, a grandmother who has prayed every morning for sixty years. Ask her what God is, and she laughs: who knows? Which one knows more? The second section of the Kena is about exactly this. The student hears yesterday's teaching and says, in effect, got it. And the teacher's reply is a paradox.
screen: `ONE CLASS, EVERYTHING FIGURED OUT.` → `SIXTY YEARS, WHO KNOWS?` → `GOT IT.`

segments.voice: The teacher says: if you think, I know it well, then surely you know very little of Brahman, only its form in you and in the gods. You'll have to think about it again. The student goes away and thinks. And comes back with this. I don't think, I know it well. And I don't think, I don't know it. Whoever among us understands that, understands it. Then the famous verse: it is known to the one who doesn't claim to know it. The one who claims to know it doesn't know. It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who don't. That can sound like a trick. It isn't. Remember yesterday: Brahman is the knower, never an object. So the moment you say, I've got it, you've turned it into an object, something in your pocket. And whatever's in your pocket isn't it. The knowing the Kena means is more like the knowing you have of being awake. You don't know it the way you know a phone number. You just are awake. Verse four gives a hint: it is known in every act of knowing, pratibodha viditam. Not a special experience, but present in each moment of awareness. And verse five raises the stakes: if you realize it here, in this life, that is the truth; if not, a great loss. The grandmother laughing, who knows? might be closer than the philosophy student. Not because she knows less. Because she isn't trying to put it in her pocket.
screen: `IF YOU THINK YOU KNOW IT WELL…` · `UNKNOWN TO THOSE WHO KNOW.` · `KNOWN IN EVERY ACT OF KNOWING.` · `HERE, IN THIS LIFE.` · then, large: `KNOWN TO THE ONE WHO DOESN'T CLAIM IT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, and try something odd: stop trying to understand. For these two minutes, you don't have to get anything. Just be aware. Notice that awareness is already here without you doing anything. You didn't have to earn it. When the mind says, is this it? am I doing it right? let that question go by. The Kena would smile at it. Come back to simply being aware. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Tomorrow the story begins. Today, the paradox that sets it up: Brahman is unknown to those who claim to know it.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when you feel sure you've got someone or something completely figured out, leave a little room. Day two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Kena 2.3, 'it is unknown to those who know', to warn students against treating Brahman as something the intellect can possess.

match.prompt: the paradox of knowing — tap the pairs.
pairs: known in every act of knowing

myth: the Kena praises the student who says 'I know it well'
the teacher says: then you know very little. think again.
verse four says Brahman is known in every act of knowing
pratibodha viditam: not a special experience, present in each moment of awareness.

fork.setup: you've just heard the teaching. the teacher asks: do you know Brahman? what does the Kena's student answer?
options: 'I don't think I know it well, and I don't think I don't know it.'
fork.reveal: neither claim. whoever understands that, the text says, understands it.

original.note: Sanskrit: avijnata, not known; Kena 2.3: unknown to those who know, known to those who don't.

trapdoor: what you thought: the paradox is a riddle with a trick answer.
what it means: Brahman is the knower, so claiming to hold it as knowledge misses it.
what a scholar hears: 2.3 reads avijnatam vijanatam vijnatam avijanatam; 2.4's pratibodha viditam is read variously as 'in every cognition' or 'through awakening'.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 2.1–2.3 (if you think you know it well; unknown to those who know)
Kena Upanishad 2.4–2.5 (known in every act of knowing; if here, the truth)

notes: Kena 2 paraphrased; check the student's reply (2.2) and the 'form in you and in the gods' of 2.1.
Pronunciation of jn in avijnata: 'gy' as commonly said in north India; some say 'gn'. Check.
The grandmother illustration is not from the text.
